profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] CyrusOne was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten, who had previously built companies acquired by IXC Communications. Wikipedia coverage of CyrusOne states the company opened what it described as the largest data center in Texas in Carrollton in 2012, the anchor of the Dallas Fort Worth cluster that this registry row is part of, alongside CyrusOne buildings in nearby Allen, Lewisville, and Collin County. CyrusOne also operates a substantial San Antonio campus and an Austin facility, both long-running Texas markets for the company, though no specific acquisition or opening story for San Antonio or Austin individually was located in available sourcing this session. The company was acquired by ABRY Partners in 2007, purchased by Cincinnati Bell for 525 million dollars in 2010, completed an IPO in 2013, and was taken private again in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts and Global Infrastructure Partners acquired it for 15 billion dollars. No building specific address or individual MW figures were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
CyrusOne DFW1 publishes 45 MW of IT capacity across 600,000 square feet of technical space in Carrollton, Texas. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 45 MW supports roughly 1,125 racks; at 10 kW per rack, a legacy colocation density, the same power supports roughly 4,500 racks. The assumption drives the answer, and CyrusOne does not publish a rack count or a per-rack power figure. The 600,000 square feet of technical space is large enough that the campus is unlikely to be running at high AI training densities throughout, but the split between AI and general workloads is not published.

The certifications tell a specific story about eligible workloads. PCI DSS qualifies the campus to host payment card processing environments. HIPAA qualifies it for regulated healthcare data. ISO 27001 certifies the information security management system against an international standard. FISMA qualifies it for certain federal government workloads. SSAE 16 Type II and TIA-942 certify the facility's operational controls and physical infrastructure design respectively against their referenced standards. Together these certifications position DFW1 for regulated enterprise workloads more than for hyperscale AI training, though nothing in the published data excludes AI use.

In Texas, this site has the third-highest published IT capacity among the eight facilities on this site that report a megawatt figure, out of 133 mapped facilities in the state total. Those eight facilities together publish 315 MW, and DFW1's 45 MW represents roughly 14 percent of that published total. Most mapped Texas facilities publish no capacity figure, so the true state total is larger and the ranking is a rank only within the visible subset. The Dallas-Fort Worth area is a major colocation market, and DFW1's scale and certification stack make it a meaningful node, but the state context does not resolve how it compares to unpublished capacity elsewhere in Texas.
